candidate: Daria Wrubel — Berkeley City Council D1
org_research: The California Working Families Party is a coalition of more than 30 grassroots organizations and labor unions with roughly 100,000 members, organized through regional chapters including the Bay Area, and governed in part by regional committees whose member representatives are elected by dues-paying members and vote in the endorsement process. Its stated priorities are economic justice, environmental protection, community safety, and countering corporate power; it claims a policy win banning AI-enabled price fixing. The party emphasizes co-governing — treating an endorsement as an ongoing accountability relationship — and asks candidates to pledge refusal of contributions from oil, law enforcement, real estate, charter school, and corporate PAC sources. This form is a combined statewide and local questionnaire, and roughly a third of its questions concern state legislative or ballot authority a city councilmember does not hold; the form's own preamble acknowledges that offices differ in power.

questions.question: Do you support raising the state minimum wage to at least $21?
questions.analysis: A statewide policy question directed at a local candidate. Raising the state minimum wage is a legislative and ballot matter, so a councilmember can take a position and advocate but cannot vote on it. Yes.

questions.question: Do you support repealing the Ellis Act?
questions.analysis: Repealing the Ellis Act requires state legislation; a councilmember can advocate but not vote. Berkeley already regulates Ellis withdrawals as far as state law permits, under BMC Chapter 13.77: relocation payments of $19,413 per household plus $6,471 for low-income, elderly, disabled, or long-tenancy households as of January 1, 2026; a ten-year right of first refusal for displaced tenants; punitive damages if a unit is re-rented within two years; a rent rollback if re-rented within five years; and a ten-year bar on condominium conversion. Withdrawal volume is low by regional standards — 508 units across 172 filings since July 1986 — which means the local answer is about closing a remaining escape hatch rather than responding to a crisis.

levers.text: Strengthen BMC Chapter 13.77 relocation payments and re-rental restrictions to the limit state law allows
Fund Rent Board monitoring of Ellis re-rentals so the ten-year right of first refusal is actually enforced
Support state legislation repealing or narrowing the Ellis Act

sources.label: BMC Chapter 13.77 — Ellis Implementation Ordinance
Berkeley Rent Board — Ellis Act Eviction
Berkeley Rent Board — 2026 Adjustments of Relocation Assistance Payments

suggested.text:
Yes.

The Ellis Act lets a landlord empty a rent-controlled building and take those units off the market permanently. Every unit withdrawn is a unit that never comes back at a regulated rent, and Berkeley has lost 508 of them since 1986.

Berkeley has gone as far as state law allows. Our Ellis ordinance requires relocation payments of $19,413 per household, plus $6,471 more for low-income, elderly, disabled, and long-tenured households; gives displaced tenants a ten-year right of first refusal; and exposes an owner to punitive damages for re-renting within two years. What we cannot do locally is stop the withdrawal itself. That is why repeal matters, and I would support it. In the meantime I would fund the Rent Board adequately enough to enforce the protections we already have, since a right of first refusal nobody monitors is not a protection.

questions.question: Do you support repealing Costa Hawkins?
questions.analysis: Repealing Costa-Hawkins requires state action, but for Berkeley the consequences are unusually concrete: the municipal code already contains dormant standby provisions written to activate on repeal. BMC 13.76.100(D) restores a rent ceiling at the most recent lawfully established rent if state law stops mandating that landlords set initial rents, which ends vacancy decontrol going forward. BMC 13.76.050(B)(1) converts the permanent post-June-1980 new-construction exemption into a rolling fifteen-year exemption. BMC 13.76.050(B)(2) self-terminates by its own terms, bringing single-family homes and condominiums under full coverage. Roughly 20,000 Berkeley units currently have regulated rents. The candidate can therefore answer this question with specific local mechanics rather than general support.

levers.text: Support state legislation and ballot measures repealing Costa-Hawkins
Keep BMC 13.76 standby trigger provisions current so they take effect immediately on repeal
Direct the Rent Board to prepare implementation guidance in advance of any repeal

sources.label: BMC 13.76.050 — Rental units partially or fully exempt
BMC 13.76.100 — Rent ceilings
Berkeley Rent Board — Rent Control 101

suggested.text:
Yes.

Costa-Hawkins is the reason Berkeley's rent stabilization ordinance protects a tenancy but not a unit. Because of it, a landlord resets rent to market the moment a tenant leaves, and everything built after June 1980 is permanently exempt. Over 20,000 Berkeley units have regulated rents, and state law caps what that regulation can actually do.

Repeal is not abstract for Berkeley. Our voters already wrote the follow-on provisions into our own code, waiting for state law to get out of the way. On repeal, Chapter 13.76 restores rent ceilings at the most recent lawful rent, ending vacancy decontrol; the permanent exemption for post-1980 construction becomes a rolling fifteen-year exemption, so newer buildings come under control as they age; and the single-family exemption ends by its own terms. I support repeal, and I would make sure the Rent Board has implementation guidance ready the day it happens rather than months after.

verification.claim: Berkeley's code contains standby provisions that activate if Costa-Hawkins is repealed
verification.note: 13.76.100(D) applies 'to the extent that state law no longer mandates that a landlord may establish the initial rental rate'; 13.76.050(B)(1) makes the new-construction exemption a rolling fifteen years on repeal or amendment of Civil Code 1954.52.

verification.note: The exemption applies 'only as long as the pertinent provisions of California Civil Code Section 1954.50 et. seq. remain in effect and require such an exemption.'

verification.claim: Scale of Berkeley's rent-regulated housing stock

questions.question: Do you support a fully funded Right to Counsel program for renters in your jurisdiction?
questions.analysis: The question's premise does not hold for this jurisdiction. Berkeley has no codified right to counsel: exact-phrase searches of the municipal code, charter, and ordinances for 'right to counsel', 'legal defense', and 'eviction defense' return no match. What Berkeley has instead is contracted eviction-defense legal services funded through Measure U1 — roughly $800,000 a year split between the East Bay Community Law Center and the Eviction Defense Center — plus the separate Housing Retention Program, which grants up to $10,000 toward rent arrears for households at or below 50% AMI and funds no legal representation at all. The 'fully funded' half of the question is also refuted: a November 2023 Council budget referral records that even after a $2 million supplement the program was expected to exhaust its funds by January 2024, against 130 eviction notices filed in September 2023 alone. Answering as though Berkeley already has a right to counsel would misstate the candidate's own city.

levers.text: Adopt an ordinance establishing an actual right to counsel in eviction proceedings, rather than contracted services
Increase and stabilize the Measure U1 anti-displacement allocation so eviction defense does not run out mid-year
Fund the Housing Retention Program at a level matched to filing volume rather than to a fixed appropriation

sources.label: City of Berkeley — Housing Retention Program
Measure U1 Budget and Forecast — FY2026 Mid-Biennial Budget Update
Budget Referral: Supplemental Funding for Housing Retention Program

suggested.text:
Yes — and I want to be precise about where Berkeley actually stands, because we do not have this yet.

Berkeley has no right to counsel. What we have is contracted eviction-defense legal services, funded at roughly $800,000 a year through Measure U1 and delivered by the East Bay Community Law Center and the Eviction Defense Center, alongside a separate Housing Retention Program that pays up to $10,000 in back rent but funds no lawyer. Good programs, but not a right: a tenant's access to representation depends on whether money is left in the contract when the notice arrives. In 2023 the Council was told the program would run dry by January even after a $2 million supplement, in a month when the Rent Board logged 130 eviction notices.

I would move Berkeley from funding services to guaranteeing representation: an ordinance establishing a right to counsel in eviction proceedings, and an anti-displacement allocation sized to filing volume instead of a fixed appropriation that runs out mid-year.

questions.analysis: Berkeley has already legislated here, and the legislative history matters more than the headline. Ordinance 7,956-N.S. added BMC Chapter 13.63 and was adopted March 25, 2025, effective April 24, 2025. RealPage sued in RealPage, Inc. v. City of Berkeley (N.D. Cal. 3:25-cv-03004-JSC) on First Amendment grounds; the City agreed not to enforce pending the preliminary-injunction motion and Ordinance 7,974-N.S. suspended the effective date. Ordinance 7,992-N.S., adopted December 2, 2025, deleted the suspension and substantially narrowed the prohibition: 'competitor data' now reaches only information not available to the general public, about properties the landlord does not own or manage, and less than 90 days old, with carve-outs for appraisal, project financing, and machine-learning model training. The narrowed ordinance is in force, carrying penalties up to $1,000 per violation per unit per month plus a private right of action. Describing Berkeley as having banned RealPage without that history would overstate what survived. I would also revive BerkDOT, which Berkeley has described as a priority since 2020 without ever creating it — traffic and parking enforcement still sit inside the police department.

questions.analysis: This is a multiple-choice question where Berkeley's actual ordinance supports the strongest option without qualification. Ordinance 7,984-N.S., adding BMC Chapter 13.114, was adopted on second reading September 30, 2025 and contains no criminal offense carve-out — no serious or violent felony list, no Penal Code 1192.7 or 667.5 exception. Its only exceptions are consent, service provision, and what state or federal law compels. This matters because state law leaves that discretion open: Government Code 7282.5 permits, but does not require, cooperation for a long list of offenses, and expressly conditions it on not violating local policy. Berkeley closes that door. Police Department Policy 415 reproduces the ordinance and states that members 'shall not transfer an individual to immigration authorities.' Berkeley also goes beyond SB 54 by binding every City agency and contractor, requiring written reporting of every ICE request to Council within ten business days, and restricting consent searches of non-public City property. Two cautions: a January 2025 council report miscites the 1986 sanctuary resolution number, and Policy 415.7.5 retains residual template language about reporting transfers that contradicts the flat prohibition — not an operative carve-out, but a hostile questioner could point at it.

levers.text: Defend and enforce BMC Chapter 13.114, including the ten-business-day Council reporting requirement
Direct removal of the residual transfer-reporting language in Police Policy 415.7.5 that conflicts with the ordinance

suggested.text:
For all cases.

Berkeley's sanctuary ordinance, adopted in September 2025, contains no criminal carve-out at all. Our police may not transfer anyone to immigration authorities, full stop, and may notify only on an outstanding criminal warrant. That was a deliberate choice. State law under SB 54 leaves cities discretion to cooperate on a long list of offenses — but it conditions that discretion on local policy, and Berkeley's policy closes it.

I support that, and I would defend it. A carve-out is not a narrow exception in practice; it is a reason for every immigrant in the city to assume that calling the police is a risk. The moment cooperation is conditional, the protection stops working for everyone.

Our ordinance also does things SB 54 does not: it binds every city department and contractor rather than just police, and it requires any ICE request to be reported to the Council in writing within ten business days. I would make sure that reporting actually happens, and I would keep our procurement clear of vendors that sell data into immigration enforcement.

questions.question: Why are you seeking the Working Families Party endorsement?
questions.analysis: An open question about motivation for seeking this specific endorsement. WFP describes its work as recruiting progressive candidates, winning policy including a ban on AI-enabled price fixing, and organizing a multiracial party, and it emphasizes co-governing. Answers that engage with WFP's particular theory of organization carry more weight than general statements of shared values.

I am seeking the Working Families Party endorsement because WFP treats an endorsement as the beginning of a relationship rather than the end of one. [Add the candidate's own reason — what drew them to WFP specifically, and any prior work with the party or its member organizations.]

[One concrete tie: WFP campaigned to ban algorithmic rent price-fixing, and Berkeley passed that ordinance and is defending it in court. Name a shared fight the candidate has actually been part of rather than one merely admired.]

questions.question: What distinguishes you as a Working Families Party candidate from your opponents?
questions.analysis: A comparative question. The distinction WFP looks for is structural — funding sources, base of support, and accountability to organizations — rather than differences in stated positions, since in Berkeley most candidates will state similar ones. Surveillance contracting is a live local fight the candidate can point to rather than a hypothetical: on May 7, 2026 the Council declined the Peace and Justice Commission's recommendation to cancel Berkeley's Flock Safety contracts over immigration data sharing, and instead adopted Resolution 72,254-N.S. extending the automated license plate reader contract twelve months for up to $200,000 with amended contract language, while separately rejecting a roughly $2 million expansion into cameras and drones. So the expansion was stopped and the underlying contract was not — the question is unresolved, and the renewal expires within the next Council term. It also sits at the intersection of three things WFP organizes on at once: corporate power, immigrant defense, and who a city does business with.

levers.text: Vote against renewing the Flock Safety automated license plate reader contract when the twelve-month extension lapses
Condition any surveillance contract on audit rights and a bar on federal access, using the Council's contracting power
Act on the Peace and Justice Commission's cancellation recommendation the Council declined in May 2026

sources.label: KQED: Berkeley extends surveillance contract with Flock Safety but rejects major expansion
NPR: Why some cities are canceling Flock license plate reader contracts
City of Berkeley — Public Financing Program

suggested.text:
This race started for me with a surveillance contract.

Berkeley calls itself a sanctuary city. We also pay Flock Safety to run automated license plate readers that photograph our neighbors' cars and feed a nationwide database. Audits in other states have since found federal agencies, including Border Patrol, searching local Flock data without the cities that owned it knowing — one state's review turned up an undisclosed pilot giving Customs and Border Protection access, and dozens of cities have cancelled their contracts since.

In May 2026 our Council had the chance to end it. The Peace and Justice Commission recommended cancelling. Instead the Council rejected the roughly $2 million expansion into cameras and drones — good — and quietly renewed the license plate reader contract anyway, twelve more months and up to $200,000. Half a decision. The renewal lapses during the next Council term, which means whoever holds this seat votes on it.

That is the difference I would name. Not that my opponents support surveillance; most of them will say they do not. It is that a sanctuary policy which stops at the boundary of a procurement decision is not a sanctuary policy. The contract is the policy. I would vote to end it, and until then I would condition it on audit rights and a hard bar on federal access.

The structural piece matters too. I am running in Berkeley's public financing program: no contribution over $60, no corporate or union money under our Election Reform Act, and no PAC money at all. Nobody with a city contract is funding this campaign.

[Add the personal specifics only the candidate can supply: what first surfaced the Flock contract for the candidate, any testimony given or organizing done around the May 2026 vote, and — if there is a real contrast — where opponents actually landed on it.]
